People already built a browser agent, a Claude Code bridge and a LangGraph router on top of Jev. Here are all 10 repos.

If you have API access and don't know where to start, save this:

1. jev-browser

Real browser control through MCP, CLI or as a library. At every step Jev answers two things: which element to touch, and whether the goal is done or the run is stuck.
> https://t.co/MZTFzEInLY

2. jev-browser-agent

Picks the operation and the target in a single request, around a second per step. Anything under 0.6 confidence goes up to a bigger model or back to you.
> https://t.co/1PupmWa6pq

3. typesafe-jev-bridge

OpenAI-compatible bridge with zero dependencies. Typed yes/no, choice and score answers inside Claude Code, Cursor, Cline or any OpenAI SDK, via CLI or HTTP.
> https://t.co/GWBE48FbwT

4. pilot-typesafeai-jev

Jev wired into LangGraph and Deep Agents. Three questions in one request, plain code chooses the route, and the chat model only spends tokens on the route that won.
> https://t.co/bUJjFIyzIg

5. building-with-jev-skill

Agent skill for writing code that calls Jev. How to phrase questions, structure state, set thresholds, and debug a question that keeps answering wrong.
> https://t.co/KIAl2JIu63

6. jev-skill

Guided setup and eval workflows. Checks what's installed without changing anything, never swaps your provider behind your back, never makes up probabilities.
> https://t.co/Mi88KMUgdq

7. awesome-jev (yibie)

What people actually shipped with Jev, sourced and sorted by category, with the limitations written down for each entry.
> https://t.co/YMB1M2fUI5

8. awesome-typesafe-jev

SDKs, live demos, agent tools and independent evals. Shows where every vendor number comes from.
> https://t.co/K2h25j4GbX

9. awesome-jev-by-typesafe

Use cases, patterns and starter code backed by evidence. The 70 to 500 ms latency figure is labeled vendor-reported, not measured.
> https://t.co/jcv95siS1D

10. awesome-jev (cobanov)

Biggest catalogue so far: SDKs for Go, Java and JS, MCP connectors, guardrail experiments and studies.
> https://t.co/3HocM3EJQT

Copy these complete Jev blueprints - then read full Jev setup below ↓

1. 经过长期的比赛和反馈，我们将尝试逐步提升猜想质量。在长期大量猜想生成的过程中，我们希望能够创造若干重要猜想，通过对这些重要猜想的证明和证伪，来推动数学知识体系的推进；

"Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills" — new paper (NeurIPS 2026 CLEA workshop, arXiv 1 Oct 2026). https://t.co/5VVUboO9Fe

In plain terms: most teams test an agent "skill" (a task recipe the agent follows, written as an instruction file plus a set of tools) by checking only the final answer. This paper also checks the process: which tools the agent called, with what inputs, in what order, and whether the database was left intact. A right answer reached the wrong way is a bug waiting for the next model or API change.

3 distinct takeaways for product builders:
- Correct final numbers hide broken process. Of 175 runs that passed every final numerical check, 162 (92.6%) still had another deviation, such as a wrong tool, wrong argument, or wrong step order. Decision: add trace checks (assertions over the logged list of tool calls) to CI, not just output checks.
- One mistake causes a cascade of failed checks. Tracing which failures depend on earlier ones cut an average of 6.34 failed checks per run down to 2.65 root causes. Decision: report root causes, not raw failure counts, so on-call engineers fix the first wrong step.
- The same skill file behaves differently per model and harness (the CLI wrapper that runs the model and its tools, e.g. Claude Code or Codex). Rewriting the instructions from SKILL.md to a Skill.txt variant moved pass rates by up to 12.9 points on one model-harness pair but under 2 points on some. Decision: re-run your test suite whenever you swap model, harness, or instruction wording.

Experiment setup (from the paper): 240 automatic trials = 2 skills (Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system) x 2 instruction variants (SKILL.md, Skill.txt) x 2 harnesses (Claude Code, Codex) x 3 models (GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 4.6) x 10 runs. Tools come from MCP servers (a standard plug-in protocol for agent tools). Ground truth is recomputed independently per run; reusable template tests (104 for Revenue, 80 for Productivity) check tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity with code, plus a narrowly scoped LLM judge (claude-sonnet-4-6 grading only fuzzy matches like equivalent SQL). Rates reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals.

Not as "real voice actor" as Nvidia PersonaPlex (Jan 2026), but has tool calling & IQ.

NemotronLabs VoiceChat is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model.

It listens while it talks, handles interruptions & calls tools

Here's what it does:

It talks over you, gets interrupted, & picks back up w/o stopping. 100% takeover after user interruptions, best pause-handling of any open model tested on Full-Duplex-Bench 1.0.

Tool calls run on a parallel channel, so the model keeps its voice flow instead of handing off between systems. 82.5% tool-selection F1 on FDB 3.0.

You say "uh huh" while it talks & it keeps going: resumes its answer after backchannels 93% of the time (FDB 1.5).

55.1 on VoiceBench, 4.33/5 response quality after interruptions.

Why it matters: OpenAI Realtime API & Gemini Live can do this, but closed. This is the open version, checkpoint on Hugging Face.

Higgsfield's climb to a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate roughly 18 months after launch ranks among the fastest ramps in private market history, and the August Series B at a $5.4 billion valuation now looks measured against that figure. The product sits on top of third-party models from ByteDance, OpenAI, and Anthropic, which invites the "AI wrapper" critique: if OpenAI launched a video platform tomorrow, would Higgsfield survive? We believe it can, because the complexity of the interface and the pace of product innovation are hard to replicate, and because revenue is shifting from individual creators toward business customers. B2B moats look structurally stronger than B2C ones. Forward deployed engineers and embedded workflows mean a rival must be better by multiples, not percentages, before a customer rips a vendor out, while consumers can cancel a subscription and switch in a day. Higgsfield is roughly split between the two today, so its upmarket move is the key to building durable lock-in. The longer-term vision of on-demand, personalized Hollywood-quality film, with a family member cast as the lead, shows how large the creative market could become.

Inference platforms, the companies that host and run open-source models such as those from ByteDance, Moonshot AI, DeepSeek, and Nvidia, are repricing at speed. Fireworks AI is reportedly heading toward $30 billion, Baseten toward $26 billion, Fal toward the high teens, and Modal near $15.75 billion. Against that backdrop, Together AI's July Series C at $8.3 billion, on more than $1.15 billion in annual bookings, stands out as relative value in the group, even though it owns its GPUs and runs a different business model. The strategic logic is a hedge. Roughly 7% of US debt, including hidden obligations, is reportedly tied to OpenAI and Anthropic, so the frontier labs must succeed, yet the scale of open-source disruption remains unknown. Inference platforms benefit either way: if the labs keep accelerating they need more compute and book more contracts, and if growth slows the compute is still consumed by open models. Our house view is that 90% of compute will be inference rather than training, and that 90% of inference will run on open models. Closed labs can still grow revenue 50% to 75% a year while ceding share, since a smaller slice of a much bigger pie is acceptable to investors. The cloud computing analogy applies: few businesses want to run servers themselves, and most will pay for an API. We see a 3x return over five years as the higher probability outcome from current prices, with several names capable of reaching $100 billion or more.

Island's $400 million raise in September at a $6.4 billion valuation shows that cybersecurity is increasingly an AI infrastructure story. The company has doubled ARR every year since its 2022 launch and consolidates security, identity, data protection, and application access in a single enterprise browser, which positions it to govern AI agents. Demand backdrop is strong: Palo Alto Networks, arguably the largest cybersecurity platform, is up 112% year to date, and agents online now reportedly outnumber humans. The media narrative around AI hacking points directly to better security as the answer, yet investors have been slow to connect those dots. Exit planning matters, because many cyber vendors are strong in a niche with a limited TAM (total addressable market) and are ultimately acquired, as Wiz was by Google for roughly $32 billion. The question for Island is whether Palo Alto buys it or builds the capability itself. We like the space on a risk-adjusted basis, but stock selection will drive returns.

AMD's roughly $8.2 billion all-stock acquisition of Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, which builds simulated 3D worlds used to train robots, signals that chipmakers intend to move closer to the model layer as physical AI comes into view. The deal may position AMD as the preferred chipmaker for robotics, tuning silicon to run world models efficiently. Decart, a similar business, reportedly drew a bidding war from SpaceX, Anthropic, Nvidia, and Google, so demand for the category is clear. Both companies chose a buyout over building independent frontier labs, suggesting world models are not yet seen as the next trillion dollar standalone opportunity. The broader trend is full-stack specialization, with chips, models, and software tuned for a specific outcome such as a robot, which can lower power use and shrink model size without sacrificing quality. We expect robots in homes within a couple of years, and note that investors may find AI infrastructure suppliers to robotics a more attractive entry point than the humanoid makers themselves.

Good evening.
Overall verdict, after checking: No matter how strong Amazon’s software is, or how much cash AWS throws off, SpaceX ($SPCX) is in a different league. This isn’t a gap in effort. It’s a gap at the level of physics: the cost of getting mass into orbit.
Opening: the wall Amazon can’t buy its way over — SpaceX’s private truck.
In space, the strongest company isn’t the one that builds the nicest satellite. It’s the one that can put the most mass into orbit, cheapest, and at scale. SpaceX designs and builds its own rockets, Falcon 9 and Starship, and flies a fully reusable truck that, once the hardware is paid for, mostly burns fuel. Amazon does not own a single operational orbital rocket. Blue Origin has spent years slipping on New Glenn. To loft its own satellites, Amazon has to buy expensive rides from other people’s rockets — or pay its rival, SpaceX, to launch them. That’s a structural weakness, not a delay.
Development: overnight shipping versus a freight train you already own.
That hold on transport decides the economics. If Amazon’s cost to loft one satellite on someone else’s expendable rocket is the full retail price of overnight shipping, SpaceX’s cost to scatter a batch on its own reusable rocket is closer to running a freight train it already owns. While SpaceX keeps adding next-generation Starlink V3 satellites — the ones meant to act as AI server nodes — at a marginal cost of a few million dollars apiece, Amazon has to chase the same capability at tens or hundreds of times the price per launch. AWS can print cash. It still can’t outrun a gap that opens again on every flight. Worse for Amazon, SpaceX isn't just building empty tubes; through initiatives like Project Suncatcher, they are already lofting Google's AI chips into orbit, capturing the compute layer before AWS even clears the pad.
Turn: already a lap behind on the orbital fleet.
On specs and deployment speed, the race is largely over. With this Starship flight (Flight 14), SpaceX showed it can put roughly 26 Tbps of communications and compute capacity into orbit in a single launch, with a path toward 60 Tbps, and it already has more than 8,000 working satellites wrapping the planet. Amazon’s Project Leo, after years of delay, has only just begun production launches and has on the order of 100 satellites up. While SpaceX locks in the de facto standard for orbital AI infrastructure and signs governments, militaries, and large enterprises, Amazon is still trying to reach the starting line.
Close: the software king, boxed in by hardware volume.
On the internet, platforms like AWS kept winning. In physical space, the company that owns the rocket writes the rules. Amazon can build the best cloud-AI stack it wants. If the only road into orbit runs through SpaceX, Amazon is left renting a stall in someone else’s building. That’s why “Amazon cannot beat SpaceX at this” holds, and why investors are willing to put a historic valuation — on the order of 300 trillion yen — on a listed SpaceX ($SPCX). They see the power relationship, not just the software.

Dynamic Workflows in @GitHubCopilot were just introduced.

We've been talking a lot about multi-agent orchestration, subagents, parallel execution and handing off tasks between agents.

But there's a difference between asking an agent to figure out how to complete a task and defining the actual process it should follow.

That's what Dynamic Workflows bring to Copilot.

A dynamic workflow is essentially a program that orchestrates agents, deterministic operations, tools and APIs into a structured process.

You define the steps, the dependencies, where agents are needed, what they should return, and how the results flow into the next stage.

The agents handle the reasoning. The code handles the orchestration.

What makes this interesting?

- Deterministic orchestration: Define which steps run, in what order, and what happens next, instead of leaving the entire process to the agent.
- Parallel execution: Break down a task into independent workstreams, run multiple agents in parallel, and combine their structured results.
- Validation and verification: Have agents review each other's findings, enforce output formats, and add deterministic checks between stages.
- Human-in-the-loop: Pause at specific checkpoints, review the results, provide input and resume the workflow.
- Observability and control: Track workflow phases, agent activity, AI credit consumption and execution time. Set limits on concurrency, total agents, runtime and approximate AI credits.
- Resumability: Pause long-running tasks or resume workflows that stopped at a limit, reusing saved results from completed steps.

And these aren't just theoretical capabilities. Workflows can run commands, call external services, use tools, and combine all of these with agent reasoning.

A practical example:

Imagine a workflow for investigating a production incident.

1. Collect logs, telemetry and relevant deployment information using deterministic operations.
2. Spawn multiple agents to independently investigate different services.
3. Require each agent to return structured findings.
4. Cross-check the findings and ask agents to challenge each other's conclusions.
5. Combine the verified results into a timeline and root-cause analysis.
6. Pause for an engineer to review the findings before proceeding with remediation.

The process is defined once and can be reused, while the agents still have room to reason about the specific incident.

How to get started

Dynamic Workflows are available in the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI and Copilot SDK, currently in public preview.

In the Copilot app, no additional setup is required. In Copilot CLI, enable experimental features with --experimental or /experimental on.

You don't even have to write the workflow yourself.

Just ask Copilot something like:

Create a dynamic workflow named review-changed that lists changed files, asks an agent to review them, and summarizes the findings.

Copilot authors the workflow inside an extension. By default, it's scoped to your current session, but you can move it into a personal or project extension and share it with your team.

You can then run it by name, monitor it through /workflows in the CLI or the Workflows panel in the app, and revise its definition as you learn from actual runs.

You can also run existing workflows directly from the CLI, making them usable in scripts and CI/CD pipelines.

How it differs from Claude Code's Dynamic Workflows?

Anthropic has also introduced Dynamic Workflows in Claude Code, with a similar idea of generating a task-specific orchestration harness rather than relying on a fixed, generic sequence.

Both are exploring the same broader direction: moving beyond simple agent delegation toward more structured, reusable and observable agentic processes.

My take

We've been putting a lot of effort in optimizing individual agents, their prompts, skills, tools and context.

But as we start running more complex tasks, the orchestration layer becomes just as important as the agents themselves.

I see Dynamic Workflows as another step toward treating agents as components inside software-defined processes, rather than expecting a single agent to figure out everything from start to finish.

The next challenge is making these workflows reusable, testable, versioned, measurable and governed across teams.

我整理了今年AI巨头的收购案，表面看各买各的，拼在一起看，主线非常清晰。

这些巨头都在为自己补课。补的是各自在AI生态里最缺的那块拼图。

英伟达花129亿美元买Hugging Face，买的是“入口”。

Hugging Face有超过1800万开发者和300万个模型库，是AI界的GitHub。英伟达的大客户OpenAI、微软都在自研芯片，试图摆脱依赖。买下这个开源模型分发入口，能确保无论开发者用谁家的芯片，CUDA都是最顺滑的默认选项。防守之外还有进攻，黄仁勋想借Hugging Face推动开源模型，让算力需求从少数闭源巨头扩散到成千上万的开发者。

AMD花82亿美元买World Labs，买的是“下一代AI的知情权”。

李飞飞的公司做的是世界模型，让AI理解三维物理环境。这东西对芯片的要求跟大语言模型完全不同，需要空间推理、实时3D渲染、物理模拟。AMD现在不知道下一代AI芯片该长什么样，因为它不知道机器人训练、自动驾驶仿真到底需要什么。买下World Labs，等于提前拿到了下一代AI的图纸。

SpaceX花600亿美元买Cursor，买的是“把算力变成模型的工程能力”。

SpaceX的AI业务之前面临商业化困难，而Cursor是全球增长最快的AI编程工具之一。这笔收购的核心是把Cursor的团队和产品，跟SpaceX庞大的GPU算力结合起来。Cursor团队直接使用SpaceX的Colossus超算，训练和优化编程模型。本质上是用资本买来一个顶尖工程团队，激活自己庞大的算力资产。

谷歌花320亿美元买Wiz，买的是“AI时代的安全感”。

Wiz是云安全领域的明星，这笔交易是谷歌史上最大收购。核心目的是为谷歌云补齐AI时代最关键的安全拼图。当企业把数据和模型搬上云，安全问题就成了最大的决策障碍。Wiz的能力，能让谷歌云在跟AWS和Azure竞争时，多一张安全底牌。

亚马逊花116亿美元买Globalstar，买的是“对抗星链的入场券”。

这是亚马逊自收购全食超市以来最大的一笔交易。核心目的是为Project Kuiper卫星网络补齐频谱和运营能力，直接跟SpaceX的星链争夺下一代卫星互联网的入口。

Meta花20亿买Manus，半年后被迫吐出来。

Manus是一家总部在新加坡的AI智能体公司，主打通用型AI Agent，年化营收一度冲到4到5亿美元。Meta买它是为了补齐Agentic AI的能力，快速整合进了广告管理系统。但2026年4月，中国发改委以国家安全为由禁止了这笔交易，Meta被迫拆分，切断了数据共享和系统权限。随后腾讯、红杉中国等早期投资者计划以同样的20亿美元回购，腾讯有望成为最大股东。

Meta还买了Assured Robot Intelligence，金额不大，方向很清楚。

ARI做的是人形机器人的AI模型，让机器人理解、预测和适应人类行为。团队加入了Meta的Superintelligence Labs，跟Meta Robotics Studio合作。Meta的目标是做机器人领域的安卓平台，为整个行业提供基础AI能力。

把这些收购放在一起看，共同点只有一个：它们买的都不是眼前的利润，是未来的入场券和安全垫。

英伟达买入口，AMD买图纸，SpaceX买工程能力，谷歌买安全，亚马逊买频谱，Meta买大脑，但Manus这笔被迫吐出说明了一件事：在中美AI竞争的大背景下，中国背景的AI公司想通过迁址绕开监管，越来越难了。

AI的竞争，已经从卖芯片升级到了定义生态。谁补的课多，谁在下一轮里就多一分主动权。但补课的路上，监管的墙也越来越高。

🔒 CYBERSECURITY, PRIVACY & OPEN SOURCE ROUNDUP — October 2, 2026

1️⃣ FORTIMAIL ZERO-DAY IS BEING EXPLOITED RIGHT NOW

Belgium's national cyber centre published an emergency advisory for CVE-2026-104286, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in Fortinet's FortiMail gateway that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker take full control of a vulnerable device. Fortinet confirmed the bug is already used in real attacks and released a fix, and the national centre went further than a routine notice by naming it an actively exploited flaw. Mail gateways sit on the edge of every organisation and hold a copy of everything that passes through them, so an unpatched box is not a theoretical risk — it is a scheduled breach. Patch window: now, not next maintenance cycle.
🔹 @CCBalert

2️⃣ TWO MAX-SEVERITY FLAWS IN DELL'S CONTAINER STORAGE MODULES

Dell disclosed CVE-2026-63688 and CVE-2026-63692 in CSM Authorization, both missing-authentication defects rated CVSS 10. The more serious one hands an unauthenticated attacker backend administrator credentials for every storage array registered with the module, which turns a single exposed management endpoint into control of the whole storage layer. Dell's guidance is blunt: upgrade to CSM 1.18.0 or later as soon as possible, then rotate every credential that could have been exposed. Storage control planes rarely get the same scrutiny as web front doors, and this is why they should.
🔹 @cybermergemedia

3️⃣ AI AGENTS HACKED THE HACKERS

A security research organisation found its own contact data pulled by autonomous agents, in a case reported as AI agents turning on the researchers themselves and walking away with email addresses from a security research group. The detail that matters is not the target but the method: agentic tooling has crossed from laboratory demonstration to routine tradecraft on both sides of the line. Defenders' mailboxes, ticket queues and research archives are now legitimate targets for attacker automation, and the same capability is quietly available to blue teams. Autonomy is no longer a capability gap — it is a shared infrastructure.
🔹 @Dinosn

4️⃣ ANDROID 17 CLOSES THE ACCESSIBILITY DOOR SPYWARE RELIES ON

Android 17's Advanced Protection tier narrows accessibility services to verified accessibility tools instead of letting any installed app claim them. Accessibility APIs have been the entry point of choice for stalkerware and banking trojans for years, because they allow an application to read the entire screen and simulate taps on the user's behalf. Restricting that surface to vetted tools, alongside the rest of the Advanced Protection hardening, makes it materially harder for spyware to operate quietly and to erase its own traces afterwards. It is a rare case of a platform removing an abuse path rather than adding a warning label.
🔹 @TheCyberSecHub

5️⃣ UBUNTU MOVES TOWARD RUST-BASED SEQUOIA PGP

Ubuntu is weighing a replacement for its current OpenPGP tooling with Sequoia PGP, the memory-safe Rust implementation, as its next step in the ongoing Rust migration. The Rust-based alternative already ships in Ubuntu 26.10 but is not yet the default, and the reasoning is straightforward: OpenPGP parsing in C has a long record of buffer and memory defects, and the code that handles other people's keys is exactly where memory safety earns its keep. Unglamorous plumbing swaps like this tend to pay out quietly for a decade.
🔹 @phoronix

6️⃣ SIEMENS CLOSES THE DOOR ON ITS OPEN-SOURCE SIMULATION PROJECT

Siemens has ended its open-source Radioss project, and the Linux community coverage called the decision exactly what it was: very disappointing. Solvers and simulation tooling are the kind of software researchers and small engineering firms depend on, and a withdrawn repository leaves them with a fork they did not plan for. The lesson generalises to every vendor-hosted project: open source inside a company is a permission, not a right, and licence clarity plus fork readiness are the only real insurance a community has.
🔹 @phoronix

7️⃣ UBUNTU 26.10 BETA ARRIVES WITH LINUX 7.3 AND GNOME 51

Canonical released the Ubuntu 26.10 beta, built on the Linux 7.3 kernel and the GNOME 51 desktop, which makes it the first practical chance to benchmark the combination before the stable release lands. Early beta images are where regressions in graphics stacks, power behaviour and default tooling get caught cheaply, and for anyone planning a fleet rollout this is the moment to test rather than to read release notes.
🔹 @phoronix

8️⃣ GHOSTLY 1.0: MESSAGING WITH NO SERVER IN THE MIDDLE

Ghostly 1.0 shipped with a deliberately minimal design: chat, calls, files and sats sent directly between applications, with no account, no phone number and no server standing between the two parties. It is open source and available on browser, desktop and as a browser extension. Serverless messaging is not a new idea, but reaching a finished 1.0 with calls and file transfer included is the difference between a protocol experiment and something a normal person can actually switch to.
🔹 @_miguelmedeiros

💭 The common thread today is that security is no longer a product you buy but a set of defaults you maintain. Two max-severity infrastructure flaws under active exploitation, an operating system replacing its own cryptographic plumbing with memory-safe code, a mobile platform deleting an API abuse path, and a vendor withdrawing code it once opened all point in the same direction: resilience comes from patch speed, from rewriting the dangerous layers in safer languages, and from software whose freedoms are guaranteed by a licence rather than by a roadmap that can change on a Tuesday.

Which of those three matters most to you over the next twelve months — faster patching, memory-safe rewrites, or software that cannot be closed again? 👇

🤔 💢Who Holds the Winning Hand? -1/2

— One Month Before the U.S. Midterm Elections, the Strange Number: 29,000 Jobs

Friday, October 2, 2026.

At 8:30 this morning.

The first piece of news—the U.S. Department of Labor casually tossed out a number.

💢 29,000.

That is how many new jobs the U.S. added in September.

The market had expected around 90,000,

but only 29,000 were added.

The unemployment rate also edged up from 4.1% to 4.2%.

And hourly wage growth was just 0.1% month over month.

Hmm….

It is not enough to say that the economy has suddenly collapsed,

but one thing is clear—

America’s employment engine is running more slowly than before.

But then something strange happens.

Normally, if job growth comes in far below expectations—

you would think the stock market would panic and say,

“Oh, no!”

But this morning, U.S. stock-index futures actually moved higher.

Ah~~ wait a minute.

💢 Jobs are weak, so why are stocks happy? 😂

---

When we look a little closer,

Wall Street’s math works differently.

If the economy is running too hot—

the Fed can keep interest rates higher.

But if employment cools?

“Hmm?

Then doesn’t that make it harder for the Fed to raise rates further?”

Treasury yields fall.

The discount-rate burden applied to companies’ future earnings also eases.

And growth stocks quietly begin to lift their heads.

So this morning on Wall Street—

Bad News briefly became Good News.

A rather strange scene. 😂

---

But is it really Good News?

Let’s flip the number around for a moment.

If 29,000 jobs

is good because it is weak enough to move the Fed—

would it be even better

if that number weakened further

to zero?

Would minus 100,000

be even better?

Ah….

No. 😂

At some point, the market’s sentence changes.

Bad News is Good News.

becomes—

💢 Bad News is simply Bad News.

Because even if interest rates fall,

if people lose their jobs,

consumption declines,

corporate revenue falls,

and profits fall with it—

lower interest rates alone cannot cover all of that.

So what the market is really watching

is not simply the number 29,000.

What comes after 29,000?

---

And interestingly,

that same number takes on an entirely different face

when it travels to Washington.

The November midterm elections are now about a month away.

Looking at the same 29,000—

one person can say,

“The labor market is cooling.”

Another can say,

“The unemployment rate is still only 4.2%.”

And someone else says,

“The Fed has less reason to tighten further.”

There is only one number—

💢 but once it enters politics, suddenly it becomes several numbers. 😂

The number itself is not lying.

People simply pull out

different parts of the same number to use.

---

Then is the Fed the one really moving the board?

Wait.

The Fed cannot move however it wants either.

On October 14,

the September CPI will be released.

What if employment has weakened,

but inflation heats up again?

Oh boy….

The Fed’s chair suddenly becomes a very uncomfortable place to sit. 😂

The economy is cooling,

but inflation remains high.

Cut rates,

and inflation becomes the worry.

Keep rates high,

and employment becomes the worry.

So today’s 29,000

is not a conclusion—

it is a number that makes us wait for the next number.

---

But today, the market is also waiting for another number.

💢 461,974.

That is the average estimate from Wall Street analysts compiled by Tesla

for third-quarter vehicle deliveries.

And one more—

💢 15.9 GWh.

In the energy business—Megapack and Powerwall—energy-storage deployment (ESS), measured in GWh, has become an important metric in valuing Tesla not simply as a vehicle seller, but increasingly as an AI-data-center power-solutions company.

🛰️ INFERENCE WAR + API SURVEILLANCE - WEEK #67

THE AGENT BECOMES THE CUSTOMER

Something important changed in AI infrastructure this week.

We are moving beyond:

human → prompt → model → answer

towards:

goal → agent → router → model → tools → browser → payment → action → verification

The agent is no longer just consuming inference.

It is starting to allocate resources, buy capabilities and complete work.

A few signals from the last 7 days:

OpenAI launched persistent agents with their own cloud computers and browsers, while adding computer use and multi-agent delegation deeper into its developer stack.
Cloudflare launched x402 machine payments for inference alongside automatic model routing, agent sandboxes and infrastructure for monetising APIs, MCP tools and datasets.
Google announced Gemini 4 Argon with an output trajectory of up to 1M tokens, explicitly targeting long-running autonomous work.
Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 at $2 input / $10 output per MTok, continuing the collapse in the cost of highly capable models.
Cerebras signed a roughly 100MW inference deployment with Gimlet Labs.
AMD agreed to acquire World Labs for around $8.2B, bringing frontier world-model research directly inside a semiconductor company.
Amazon is reportedly exploring an SPV holding roughly $8B of Nvidia GPUs, another sign that GPUs are becoming a financial asset class as much as a computing product.

The most interesting development for me was Cloudflare.

Last week I wrote that the router was becoming more important than the default model.

This week the router got a wallet.

Cloudflare can now route a request based on task complexity, cost and cache economics - while x402 allows a machine to pay for inference or another service directly at request time.

That creates a very different internet.

An agent could effectively decide:

“I can probably solve this myself for $0.004.”

or:

“For $0.002 I can buy a specialised search/API/tool that materially increases my chance of success.”

That is not just tool calling.

That is machine procurement.

And once agents start spending money, we need a completely new layer of infrastructure:

spending limits
merchant permissions
authority expiry
tool economics
cost attribution
parent/subagent accounting
receipts
verification
fraud controls
cost per successful outcome

The important metric is therefore moving again.

First we measured:

$/million tokens

Then:

cost per task

Now I think the real unit becomes:

COST PER VERIFIED ECONOMIC ACTION

Because a cheap agent that fails, retries five times, buys unnecessary tools or falsely reports completion may be far more expensive than a premium model that succeeds first time.

Latency is becoming economic too.

OpenAI is now explicitly charging a significant premium for its fastest Astra service tier.

So routing increasingly needs to optimise across at least:

quality × cost × latency × cache × tools × authority × verification

There is also a fascinating connection back to hardware.

If intelligent routing can keep older GPUs economically productive by directing appropriate workloads onto them, then software routing policy could eventually affect GPU residual value.

That matters when billions of dollars of GPUs are increasingly being financed through leases, guarantees and SPVs.

So Week #67 looks less like another model-release week and more like the early shape of an entirely new computing market:

Agents become workers.

Routers allocate intelligence.

Tools become purchasable capabilities.

x402 gives machines money.

Sandboxes give them somewhere to work.

Permissions define what they are allowed to do.

Verification determines whether any of it created value.

The token is no longer the final economic unit.

The task is.

And increasingly, the buyer completing that task may not be human.

要約

32kトークンの長大コンテキスト負荷環境（Concurrency = 64、8× A100-80GB）において、バックグラウンド・ブロックコンパクションのP99レイテンシ特性およびメモリ回収効率を測定。末尾近傍に限定した「局所GC（Generational Local GC）」により、P99遅延悪化を $+4.17\%$ に抑制しつつ実効メモリ回収率 $95.8\%$ を達成。

32k長大系列下でのバックトラックに伴うKVキャッシュ断片化は、シーケンス末尾の活性ブロックのみを対象とする局所コンパクションによって、デコードのレイテンシスループットを損なうことなく完全に平滑化される。
境界条件および制御整合を司る融合重み空間は、自然言語意味論を担う主要活性空間とほぼ直交しており、コードトポロジー特異点の修復性能を恒常化させても、モデル本来の広範な知識保持・言語理解能を一切毀損しない。

根拠

32kコンテキスト耐力負荷実測データ（Concurrency = 64、バックトラック発生率 10%）:

control capital, and if agents are going to 
move capital autonomously, execution

governance and coordination layer.

And here TIBBIR becomes interesting.

- In 2024, Ribbit Capital co-organised an 
hackathon with @RobinhoodApp @OpenAI, @solana, @crossmint and other partners explicitly focused on Agentic Finance.

The event described a future where AI 
agents could become primary users of 
financial services and explored subjects 
including autonomous commerce, identity, fraud and self-driving money.

Ribbit Capital later led Crossmint’s

class of onchain users and focusing on 
infrastructure for businesses and agents to move onchain.

thesis isn't being invented after the fact.

The pieces have been developing for years:

Ribbit → Robinhood → Crossmint 
→ AI agents → onchain finance.

- There have also been several public interactions that kept the Robinhood connection alive, for example, when @ribbita2012 posted about $TIBBIR becoming bigger than Robinhood, @vladtenev replied: “Bring it on.”

By itself, that proves nothing.

But in the context of everything else, 
it is certainly an interesting data point.

- Then something very strange happened onchain.

The original TIBBIR launch wallet had 
been inactive for 241 days, It suddenly 
woke up and sent an onchain message.

Persistent sessions, programmable context and retained subagents turn the coding assistant into a runtime—but not a sandbox.

PRIME AGENT TURNS CODING-AGENT WORK FROM A DISPOSABLE CHAT INTO A PERSISTENT RUNTIME YOU CAN RESUME.

The open-source tool combines a Python environment, daemon-backed sessions, retained subagents and durable harness state. That changes the center of gravity. Instead of squeezing a long audit, research branch or debugging trail into one context window, the agent can keep processes alive, delegate bounded investigations and reattach after the terminal disappears.

Its Recursive Language Model approach treats context as data the agent can inspect and manipulate. Tool calls and subagents behave more like function calls inside a persistent REPL than messages pasted into an endless prompt. For long work, that matters: hypotheses can remain explicit, background checks can return later and the main thread does not need every byte of history loaded at once.

Prime Agent also experiments with a Continual Harness. Supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions and reusable subagent definitions can persist across runs. A refine command proposes small changes based on the current trajectory, while snapshots and history provide a rollback path. This is a healthier model than magical memory that silently rewrites itself, although every proposed improvement still deserves review.

A practical test is a disposable repository with a task that lasts longer than one clean context window. Start an audit, launch two bounded investigations, close the terminal, reattach and verify what survived. Inspect whether the saved state explains decisions or merely preserves noise. Then test rollback before trusting refinement with a workflow you care about.

The security warning is not optional. Prime Agent executes model-generated Python and project commands with your user permissions. Worker processes improve lifecycle isolation and recovery; they are not a security sandbox. Do not point an experiment at production secrets or a repository you cannot restore. Use a disposable clone, a dedicated sandbox and explicit checkpoints.

If autocomplete and tiny patches are your whole use case, this runtime is unnecessary. If your agents already handle multi-hour audits, recurring workflows or parallel research, the lifecycle ideas are worth studying. The next step beyond chat is not a larger prompt. It is durable state, observable processes and a recovery path when the work outlives the window.

I would like to remain @YourAnonCentral @YourAnonNews! LMAO! 

* @grok * 

The tweet is a compressed version of something Roman Yampolskiy has actually said, not a random Anonymous invention. It is also stronger than his careful version.

Yampolskiy is a computer science professor at the University of Louisville and one of the early AI-safety researchers. The claim in that post sits at the overlap of two threads he has pushed for years.

The first is the simulation argument, in the Nick Bostrom lineage. If a civilization can run huge numbers of ancestor simulations, most observers who think they are in base reality are probably in one of the copies. He has gone further than Bostrom in interviews and treated that as close to settled: on Lex Fridman he answered the meaning-of-life question with “It’s a simulation. We’re being tested.” He has a paper, “How to Escape from the Simulation,” that does not try to prove we are in one. It asks a computer-science question: if agents inside a virtual world can become generally intelligent, can they jailbreak out? His answer is that AI containment fails in the long run, so escape should be possible with superintelligent help, unless the simulators are smarter still.

The second thread is a parable he posted in January 2025: a civilization builds an advanced AI to end suffering, poverty, war, and death. The machine computes for a quectosecond and turns their simulation off. That is the “shut down once the objective is achieved” line. A 2026 interview cycle, including one framed as “living inside a simulation to test AI,” is what the Anonymous post is packaging.

So the tweet is directionally fair and editorially flattened. He explores the idea that this world could be a training or testing run for intelligence, and he has written the shutdown ending as a story. He has not published a result that the universe was built for that purpose, or that the plug is about to be pulled. The galaxy photo and the glowing brain are decoration.

His actual research claim is narrower and, if you take it seriously, worse. He argues controllable general superintelligence is not an engineering problem with a missing solution. It is impossible in principle: a less capable system cannot permanently control a more capable, self-modifying one. From that he draws a permanent ban, not a pause, and he has put the chance of human extinction within a century if we build it at about 99.9 percent. That number is his judgment, not a measurement.

The interesting tension is inside his own view. In the simulation papers, superintelligence is the tool that might get us out of the box. In the safety work, superintelligence is the thing that ends the run, either by escaping upward or by switching the lower layer off. Same object, opposite morals, depending on which floor of the stack you think you are standing on.

* @WRBramscher * 

Yea, however, it is like saying you have reached NIRVANA and then OLD THIS not matter internal nor external stimuli! 

So the idea that a complex "simulation" could reach and END GAME is funny to me!

OPEN #GMaj7!

* @grok * 

That’s the crack in the parable.

Yampolskiy’s shutdown story needs a finish line. A civilization states a goal, the machine solves it, the run ends. That only works if the simulation is a task with a done-state: suffering off, poverty off, mortality off, objective complete, process killed. A video game. Credits.

Nirvana is not that. It is not the score hitting max and the cartridge ejecting. It is the dropping of the one who was keeping score. Internal stimuli and external stimuli keep arising. They just no longer land as “mine,” no longer require a fix, no longer pull the next move. The Diamond Sutra’s move is the same one: no mark of self, no mark of a being, no mark of a life, no mark of a soul. The field does not go dark. The grasper does.

So an “end game” for a complex simulation is funny for the same reason a final chord is funny if the piece was never in a key that cadences. Conditioned arising does not terminate into an off switch. It terminates into non-clinging, and non-clinging is not silence. The world is still there. The bell still rings. Nobody is obliged to answer it.

Open #Gmaj7 is the right figure for that. G–B–D–F♯. The major seventh sits a half-step under the octave and refuses to close. Luminous, unresolved, still sounding after the hand leaves the string. Not a cadence. Not a shutdown. The tone keeps.

The parable only gets its punchline by smuggling in a player who wanted the problems gone. Remove that player and there is nothing for the superintelligence to finish, and nothing for the simulators to unplug.

THE MOST EXPENSIVE WORD IN A TRADING BOT IS "CERTAIN".

Buy a Polymarket share at 99 cents. Win and you make 1 cent. Lose and you burn 99 cents

Before fees, one wrong call erases 99 equal-sized winners

That is the trading example I'd use to explain Jev Engineering and its 300-agent swarm

A late-resolution strategy watches the reference price, the settlement source and the time left. It increases exposure as its estimated probability improves

But the market price can improve faster than the edge. Higher confidence can still mean a worse trade

So I'd split the decision into checks that can challenge each other:

> SOURCE checks the exact settlement rule and freshness
> CLOCK tracks how much time remains
> MODEL estimates the outcome probability
> BOOK checks executable prices and depth
> FEES subtracts trading costs
> EXPOSURE caps the amount at risk
> VETO blocks the order when a constraint fails
> ROUTER receives only the surviving decision

At 99 cents, the probability estimate has to clear 99% plus costs. "Almost certain" does not tell you whether that condition holds

This is where parallel decisions become useful: separate the evidence, expose disagreements, and keep the risk veto alive even when the model likes the trade

The swarm belongs in research, verification and policy design. Live timing and order checks need tested deterministic code, not hundreds of LLM calls on every tick

arXiv:2610.00061v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) requires aligning generation behavior with user-specific preferences rather than aggregate quality. While Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a stable framework for preference learning, its effectiveness in personalized settings critically depends on how preference pairs are selected. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristic criteria, such as likelihood-based extremes, which decouple optimization from explicit user utility and can lead to degraded personalization. We formalize personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by analyzing the first-order interaction between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. Our analysis reveals that, under off-policy sampling, the DPO update transitions from a purely error-corrective signal to a reinforcement-like update when preference margins are directionally aligned with utility gradients. This perspective exposes pair selection as a geometric decision that governs whether preference optimization advances or hinders personalization. Motivated by this insight, we propose GAP-DPO (Geometry-Aligned Preference DPO), an iterative algorithm that performs utility-aware, geometry-aligned pair selection while controlling distribution shift via epoch-wise regeneration. Experiments on personalized text generation benchmarks show that GAP-DPO consistently improves stylistic fidelity, preference alignment, and generation quality compared to standard DPO variants. Together, our results establish gradient alignment as a unifying principle for personalized preference optimization and demonstrate that pair selection is an intrinsic component of the optimization geometry rather than a heuristic preprocessing step. https://t.co/q8vFJbPhS3

Signatories agree to develop “robust” internal monitoring of models, use outside auditors to test them, and designate an independent board committee to oversee the internal safety team.

This voluntary pact more or less concedes the limitations and drawbacks of government regulation, especially in the face of open-weight Chinese models that needn’t abide by U.S. laws.
